title: Chanura Challenges Krishna and Balarama
story:
The rejoicing had not yet settled when a wrestler walked out into the centre of the arena and raised his hand for quiet. His name was Chanura, the strongest of Kamsa's champions, and the crowd, which had been chanting only a moment before, knew at once what was coming.

He called out to the two brothers by name, and his words were smooth. "Son of Nanda," he said, "and Rama — you two are counted among heroes. And those who do what pleases the king find their own welfare in it. The cowherds, after all, are always cheerful, as everyone can plainly see. So let us, both you and I, do what will please the king today."

It was an invitation dressed as a courtesy, and everyone in the arena understood what it really asked. Chanura was leading the two boys toward a match with the king's wrestlers — men trained to kill, men for whom the ring was not sport but work. He spoke of pleasing the king as if pleasure and death were the same thing in that place, and the crowd's noise fell away as it waited to hear how the two would answer.

Krishna's reply, the verses say, was fitted to the place and the moment, and it was more careful than Chanura's challenge deserved. He did not refuse the fight, and he did not call it a trap, though it was. He simply stated what was true. We are subjects of this lord of the Bhojas, he said, but we are forest-dwellers — boys who grew up among the cows. We are children. A boy plays with boys of his own strength; that is what is proper. Let it be a fair match, and we will gladly make sport.

There was a weight in that answer that Chanura, for all his size, did not seem to feel. He was a wrestler who had made his name by breaking the men he was set against, and he would not be turned aside by the word of a boy. He answered that the fight must go forward, that the strong ones were waiting, and that there was no injustice in any of it — he himself would meet Krishna, and Mushtika would face Balarama.

High above the ring, Kamsa did not speak. He had arranged this whole day, and now his champion was arranging the last of it for him, pressing the two boys toward the match that was meant to end them. He leaned forward on his throne and watched, and said nothing.

So the terms were set, not by the two young men but by the man who could not see what he was asking for. Chanura had framed the match as a favour to the king and a kindness to the crowd. In pressing it on two boys who had asked only for equals, he had done something simpler and more dangerous: he had made it plain, to everyone watching, which side had begun with the unfairness. The wrestlers took their places, and the arena held its breath.
reflection: Krishna's answer is a small lesson in restraint. He does not refuse the fight; he names its rules — that they are boys, that equals should meet equals. It is Chanura, the champion, who insists on the unfair match, and in doing so he only tells the whole arena whose cause is the just one.
next_story_tease: The match itself was about to begin.
hero_scene: Chanura, the great wrestler, striding into the centre of the Mathura arena to challenge the two boys, Krishna and Balarama standing calm and unhurried before him as the hushed crowd leans down from the galleries.
visual_elements: wrestlers waiting at the ring's edge
